title: Strategy by Draft Stage: Early, Middle and Late
brief: What should we prioritize in the early, middle and late parts of our auction: stable PTS, REB and AST early, value in the middle tier, and upside flyers at the end? It must cover how the cost of a mistake shrinks further down the board, when to take safe players versus upside, and when position needs start to matter.
summary: Spend the early part of the auction on proven high scorers and assist men, because points and assists are the hardest stats to find later and early mistakes cost the most. Hunt value among players ranked roughly 51 to 100, and start checking positions around the 85th to 108th player off the board. Fill your last three or four roster spots with upside flyers, not steady veterans you could pick up on waivers.

sections.heading: How our auction maps to draft rounds

paragraphs.text: The expert notes talk in snake-draft rounds and pick numbers. Our league drafts 144 players across 12 teams, so one round equals 12 players. Round 1 is the top 12 players bought, round 3 is players 25 to 36, round 6 is 61 to 72, and round 10 is 109 to 120. Our draft ends at player 144, which is the end of round 12. Advice about rounds 13 and 14 covers players who will be on our waiver wire. In this article, early means roughly the first 36 players bought, middle means about 37 to 100, and late means about 100 to 144.

League size changes what a slot is worth. In a 12-team league, an average player is about the 75th ranked player. A player who is close to average in every category can still finish around 100th. So a player near rank 100 is not a building block for us. He is a filler.

sections.heading: The cost of a mistake shrinks down the board

paragraphs.text: Gaps between slots are large at the top and small at the bottom. The gap between the 1st and 20th player is huge. The gap between the 50th and 70th is small. Overpaying for a player who goes 20 spots too high in round 3 is bad. Going 15 spots too high in round 6 hardly matters. In practice, be strict about price on the top 36 players and relaxed about small overpays after about player 60.

Small misses do not matter even early. Buying a player as the 10th best who finishes 15th or 17th is fine. A big miss does matter, such as buying the 11th best and watching him finish 30th. The real early risk is a big reach on a player who has almost no chance to earn his price.

Top players are also stable. Over five seasons, about 16 of the 9-cat top 25 repeated the next year. 75% of top 10 players stayed in the top 25. Every healthy top 25 player who dropped out still finished inside the top 50. So the floor of a healthy early buy is high. Unexpected injuries, not draft order, are what swing leagues.

Further down, ranks are packed tightly. A small drop in one stat can cost a player 10 or more spots. That is why the gap between rank and expected finish needed to count as real value gets wider down the board. Late, only buy a player if he could beat his slot by a lot.

sections.heading: Early: stable points and assists, broad value

paragraphs.text: Points is the most stable and predictable category. Points and assists are very hard to find in volume later. FT% is also scarce later. If you want to compete in these, buy them with your early dollars. A low-scoring, low-usage player as your top buy nearly commits you to punting points. A low-assist player early can leave you behind in assists, because big assist players are rare late.

Do not swing too far the other way. This is not a points league. Do not pay early for a player whose value is mostly points. Avoid two-category players early, because they leave holes you must fix later. Players elite only in blocks, FG% and rebounds get overpaid in category leagues. Do not buy them at round 3 prices, which means players 25 to 36. A defense-only, poor-shooting player early can leave you far behind in points and threes.

Among the top 12, treat the big names as a group of roughly equal options. Rankings are ordinal. Number 6 is not much better than 8 or 12. If another manager outbids you on your target, move to the next one in that group. Do not lock onto a planned pair of players. Your first four buys and then your first eight need to make sense together. The 7 or 8 player core is what matters.

Schedule only matters for your first three rounds of players, roughly your first three buys. For those players, check the schedule for our playoff weeks 19, 20 and 21, ending 2027-03-28. One expert does not want his best player to have a two-game week in the semifinals or final. For later buys, ignore the schedule.

The best value is usually found between the 51st and 100th player. Players there can beat their expected rank by 10 to 40 spots. This is where to bid on players the room is underrating. If a player is going well below his value, buy him and adjust your build later. Do not plan a punt in the early stage. Focus on value and lean into a punt later if one appears.

Draft for stats and statistical shapes, not positions. Positions only become a focus around round 8 or 9. For us that means around the 85th to 108th player off the board, which is usually your 8th or 9th roster spot. At that point, check two things. Can you fill G, G, G, F, F, F and C? Which categories are you losing? Then fill needs, such as a big man for rebounds. Sometimes you will pay a little early just to get assists.

Boring veterans are bad buys in the early and middle stages. Do not pay for safe, low-upside players just to top the projected standings in the draft room. Take a veteran only if he falls well below his value.

sections.heading: Late: upside flyers and money management

paragraphs.text: Leagues are won by players who beat their price by a lot. A safe player who finishes at his draft slot means nothing. From round 10 on, about the 109th player in our auction, buy upside. Use at least three of your last four roster spots on flyers who could beat their slot by 40 to 50 places. Each late buy should have top 70 upside, and ideally top 50. Prefer a young player or rookie with upside over a proven player with a known, limited ceiling.

The downside of most late buys is just being useless, and that costs little. Do not buy a player around 110 who projects to finish 110th. That value sits on the waiver wire. A streaming slot is worth about a top 100 player. You usually drop and stream your round 10 to 13 picks anyway. With daily lineups, FAB and 6 adds per week, a failed flyer is easy to replace. Steady veterans that experts call value outside the top 150 will be free agents in our league.

Late, target players with top-30 upside even if they carry injury risk. If they miss long stretches, move on. A late buy can also be insurance on a star, by taking a teammate who should start. Have a reason for every buy: what the upside is, and how likely he is to beat the alternatives.

Keep some budget for the end of the auction. If you spend everything early, you cannot compete for late bargains. A team with a few extra dollars can snipe your 1 USD nominations. Keep flexible lists with large groups of flyer targets, not one name per spot. Once you are in flyer territory, buy the flyers. Do not try to time ADP to wait for them.

Safe or upside late. Most notes say the last spots should always be flyers, especially in a 12-team league. Others say it depends on your roster. If you have already taken several injury risks or flyers, lean late toward steady players with a narrower range. If you took no risks early, take a flyer later. Our rule: before your last four buys, count your risky players. If you have three or more, one steady player is fine. Otherwise, go all upside.

Reaching and punting. One view says if you miss points, assists or FT% early, just punt them. Another warns that managers overindex on punting and should chase value early. On reaching, one expert accepts paying a little early to fill a need like assists. Others say never lock onto must-have players and avoid big reaches. The common ground: small overpays to fix a category are fine in the middle and late stages, where mistakes are cheap. Big reaches in the top 36 are not.
